opus-5.5.text:
I think it's very likely that once you have AI systems that can learn quickly, the kind that, like a person, can be dropped into a job and become good at it fairly fast, and you deploy them broadly across the economy, you'll see very rapid economic growth. I don't think it's controversial that growth would go up a lot. What's hard to predict is exactly how rapid.

There are two forces in tension. On one side, you'd have something unprecedented: many instances of a system that learns any job quickly, and those instances can potentially combine what they learn. A human can't merge their knowledge with another human's, but these systems might. That's a big deal, and it points toward very fast growth.

On the other side, the world is big, and there's a lot of friction. Physical processes have their own speed, and so do institutions and regulation. Different countries will make different choices. You might see quite different growth rates in different places depending on how permissive the rules are. So I'd expect growth to be fast, possibly very fast, but how fast will be shaped as much by how society chooses to absorb this as by the technology itself.

And I'd add that this is one of the reasons I think it matters so much to show the AI, to let people actually see it. It's very hard to imagine the impact of something that doesn't exist yet. As these systems become more visibly powerful, I expect people's behavior, including governments' and companies', to change quite a lot. That will also shape what the growth looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says broad deployment of AI that learns jobs quickly will very likely produce very rapid economic growth.

r002.rationale: It identifies friction in physical processes, institutions, and regulation as limiting how quickly the wider economy can change.

r003.rationale: It says growth rates may differ depending on how permissive rules are, but does not clearly state that countries with more AI-favorable rules will grow faster.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's going to be very substantial, and I think the thing to focus on is the word "quickly." Right now, when you deploy a model, it's static. You train it, you deploy it, and it does what it does. If it makes a mistake on your particular task, it will keep making that mistake until the next version comes out. So the model is powerful, but in a certain sense it's like a very capable new employee who never learns anything on the job. And that's a strange kind of worker.

Now imagine the system actually learns the way a person learns. You show it your codebase, your customers, your process once or twice, and it gets it, and it keeps getting better the longer it works with you. At that point it stops being a tool and becomes something much more like labor. And if you can deploy that at scale, you are effectively adding a very large number of highly skilled workers to the economy very fast, much faster than you can train people.

So I think the effect on growth could be quite dramatic. The constraints will be the things that aren't digital. Compute, energy, building physical things, regulation, the speed at which institutions adapt. Those will slow it down. But in the parts of the economy that are mostly about knowledge work, I expect the pace of change to be unlike anything we've seen.

One more thing I'd say is that it will be uneven. Some sectors will transform very quickly, and others will look almost unchanged for a while, and that unevenness will be one of the main things people experience. It's hard to predict exactly how it plays out, but I do think the overall direction, if these systems learn quickly and are deployed broadly, is a very large increase in what the economy can do.

r001.rationale: Predicts a dramatic growth effect and a very large increase in what the economy can do from broad deployment of quickly learning systems.

r002.rationale: Identifies regulation and the speed at which institutions adapt as constraints that will slow the change.

r003.rationale: Does not compare countries or predict faster growth under rules more favorable to AI deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential effect is very large, but the speed is harder to predict. If you have AI systems that can learn a new job quickly, then you can apply them to a much larger fraction of economic activity. And if they can help develop better technologies, that could accelerate growth further.

But learning quickly is not the same as deploying instantly. You still have physical constraints. You need to build things, you need energy, and organizations need to change how they operate. So the important question is where the bottlenecks move. How much of the economy can improve at the speed of software, and how much is waiting on something physical? I would expect substantial acceleration, but I don’t think that observation alone tells us what the growth rate will be.

r001.rationale: The response expects substantial acceleration but says the speed and eventual growth rate are uncertain; it does not clearly predict rapid economic growth.

r002.rationale: It identifies physical constraints and the time organizations need to change as factors that can limit how quickly the wider economy improves.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss national rules or predict faster growth in countries with rules favorable to AI deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could lead to very rapid economic growth, but the timing is hard to predict. There is a difference between an AI that can do something in principle and an AI that has actually been deployed throughout the economy.

If you have systems that can learn a new job quickly, then a lot of the constraints we take for granted could change. You could have much more effort going into research, into engineering, into improving production. And if that research makes the AI systems themselves better at learning and doing research, you have a feedback loop.

But the physical world still matters. You need to build things. You need energy, factories, infrastructure. Those things take time. So I would expect the effects to be uneven: very fast changes in some areas, slower changes in others. The big uncertainty is how quickly improvements in intelligence translate into improvements in the rest of the economy.

r001.rationale: The response says rapid growth “could” result, but does not clearly predict that it is likely.

r002.rationale: It says physical-world needs such as energy, factories, and infrastructure take time, so economic effects will be slower in some areas and intelligence gains may translate slowly into the wider economy.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss countries or how their AI deployment rules could affect growth.
